extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of economic institutions
extracted.subtask_short: classical political economy: land and towns
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical political‑economy principles governing the relationship between agriculture, manufactures, towns, land tenure, and incentives for improvement. Describes historical institutions (primogeniture, entails, slavery, tenant forms), their effects on cultivation, and the sequence of capital allocation (agriculture → manufactures → foreign commerce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of agriculture for town subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivation and improvement of the country, which affords subsistence, must necessarily be prior to the increase of the town; the surplus produce of the country, or what is over and above the maintenance of the cultivators, constitutes the subsistence of the town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towns can only increase in proportion to the surplus produce of the surrounding (or supplying) country; even when subsistence is imported from distant countries, that does not contradict the general rule. The town’s growth depends on rural productivity and surplus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital allocation preference toward land when profits equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon equal, or nearly equal profits, most men will choose to employ their capitals rather in the improvement and cultivation of land than either in manufactures or in foreign trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: capital fixed in land is more under the owner’s view and command and less liable to accidents or to the uncertainties of distant trade and human folly; personal preferences for country life, tranquillity, and independence also attract capital to land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of landed capital vs merchant capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital of the landlord, fixed in the improvement of his land, seems to be as well secured as the nature of human affairs can admit of; the fortune of the trader is much more liable to accidents and to human folly and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investments that are physically present and under the owner’s control are seen as safer, which shapes investment choices and thus economic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban growth driven by clustering of artisans and rural demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers (smiths, carpenters, masons, etc.) naturally settle near one another and form small towns; the town is a continual fair or market, to which the inhabitants of the country resort to exchange their rude for manufactured produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towns grow as artisans and retailers locate together to serve farmers’ occasional needs; the quantity of finished work sold to the country regulates the materials and provisions they buy, so town employment and subsistence grow only as rural demand expands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of uncultivated land deters export-oriented manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: In North American colonies, where uncultivated land is still to be had on easy terms, no manufactures for distant sale have been established; when an artificer acquires surplus stock he buys and improves land rather than establishing distant-sale manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opportunity cost: where land is available and attractive, labor and capital move to agriculture rather than manufacturing for export; artisans become planters and prefer the independence and higher subsistence of landowning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land scarcity encourages manufacturing for distant sale and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries where there is either no uncultivated land or none on easy terms, artificers who acquire surplus stock prepare work for more distant sale; manufactures become subdivided and refined in many ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of land opportunity channelizes capital into manufactures and trade, which over time leads to specialization and improvement in manufacturing techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural sequence of capital deployment: agriculture → manufactures → foreign commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the natural course of things, the greater part of the capital of every growing society is, first, directed to agriculture, afterwards to manufactures, and, last of all, to foreign commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the expected developmental order in a society with territory; exceptions occur where historical institutions or political arrangements invert the sequence (e.g., foreign commerce introducing manufactures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign commerce and historical institutions can invert natural order
rubrics_metrics.description: In modern European states this natural order has often been inverted: the foreign commerce of some cities introduced fine manufactures fit for distant sale, and manufactures and foreign commerce sometimes gave birth to agricultural improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical contingencies and institutions (manners, customs, government forms) can force societies into an unnatural and retrograde order of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing of uncultivated lands and concentration of ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: When barbarian chiefs usurped lands after Rome’s fall, great tracts of uncultivated land were engrossed by a few great proprietors; primogeniture and entails prevented their division and perpetuated large estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrated ownership plus rules preventing division hinder the redistribution of land that might encourage cultivation and improvement; legal regime of succession matters for land use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primogeniture and entails hinder land improvement and share injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of primogeniture and the introduction of entails precluded dividing estates by succession or alienation; though once defensible for security, they have become contrary to the real interest of numerous families and obstructive to improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These institutions persist to support family pride and noble privileges but prevent more equitable and productive division of land; entails especially bind property across generations to sustain elite monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large proprietors’ misaligned incentives reduce improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Great proprietors are seldom great improvers: in disorderly times they defended territories rather than improved land, and later often lacked inclination, ability, or capital to improve estates; their tastes lead to ornament rather than profitable improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners of great estates may spend on embellishing a small area around their house at disproportionate cost and avoid profitable, incremental improvements across the estate; personal preferences and expense patterns matter for investment in land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slave labour is the dearest and least productive form for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The work done by slaves, though it appears to cost only their maintenance, is in the end the dearest of any: a person who can acquire no property will labour as little as possible and produce no improvement beyond subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence (Pliny, Columella, Aristotle) shows cultivation under slave management degenerates; where cultivation requires incentives to raise output beyond maintenance, slavery fails to deliver improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metayer (coloni partiarii) arrangement limits tenant investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietor furnishes seed, cattle, instruments; produce divided (often half); tenants being freemen have interest to maximise produce but not to invest their own saved stock because the proprietor would claim half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While metayers cultivate at proprietor’s expense and have some incentive to increase output, they will not combine their own capital with the proprietor’s because gains are shared—thus improvement beyond what owner’s stock allows is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of tenure and long leases encourage tenant improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: When farmers have leases for terms of years and security against arbitrary ouster (e.g., action of ejectment), they may find it in their interest to lay out capital to improve the farm because they can expect to recover investment before the lease ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal protections that make tenant possession secure and long enough (long leases, freehold-like tenure) encourage investment; differences in national law (England vs. France/Scotland) affect incentives to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes, tithes, and excessive public/private services discourage improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The tithe (a tenth) is a very great hindrance to improvement and a tax amounting to half would be an effectual bar; public services, purveyance, taille and irregular oppressive taxes make it disadvantageous to employ stock in land improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes measured against presumed profits induce tenants/proprietors to conceal stock or avoid using accumulated stock on land; taxes and compulsory services divert or destroy incentives to invest in long-term improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on internal trade (anti-engrossing, market privileges) obstruct cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions on exportation of corn without licence and restraints upon inland commerce (laws against engrossers, regraters, forestallers, privileges of fairs and markets) obstruct cultivation and the efficient distribution of produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade regulations that prevent free circulation and sale of agricultural produce reduce market incentives and thereby diminish cultivation and improvement (example: ancient Italy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative improvement: proprietors vs tenant farmers vs slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors generally improve more rapidly than tenant farmers on account of retained profits; tenant farmers’ improvements are slower because rent consumes a share; slaves and owners who use slave labour produce least improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where tenants can become owners or where farmer-proprietors exist, they become principal improvers; institutional and cultural factors (respect for yeomanry, political franchises) affect attractiveness of farming and the flow of stock into agriculture.
